title: Slave-making in ants arose from capturing pupae as food

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Slave-making in ants arose from capturing pupae as food

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The slave-making instinct of ants arose when pupae of other species, originally collected as food, were reared and proved useful as workers, and natural selection strengthened this habit until some species became wholly dependent on slaves.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the habit of collecting pupæ originally for food might by natural selection be strengthened and rendered permanent for the very different purpose of raising slaves.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VII, “Instinct”; section “Slave-making ants”. Scope: slave-making (dulotic) ants such as Formica sanguinea and Polyergus rufescens

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch07-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.53

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The transition is operationalizable through comparative reconstruction. Public centralized data cover taxonomy and phylogeny better than the decisive behavioural sequence.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Code predation on pupae, facultative brood capture, worker integration, and obligate dulosis across ant phylogenies, then reconstruct transition order. A progression from food collection to useful rearing supports the claim; different ancestral behaviour opposes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Behavioural states and fitness consequences require literature compilation.

Multiple origins may have followed different routes.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Ant taxonomy and trees are public, and the living grade from Formica to Polyergus is exactly the comparison Darwin used, so a partial phylogenetic test is realistic. Habit coding is incomplete outside the well-studied genera, and the original purpose of the raids is not a character in any database. The analysis would take months of literature harmonization rather than a short standard run.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map predation on pupae, facultative slave-making, and obligate dulosis on an ant phylogeny focused on Formica and Polyergus. The claim is supported if dependent slave-makers are derived from raiders that still use foreign brood as food; it is weakened if dulosis is ancestral or arises without a predatory-raiding precursor.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Behavioral states are unevenly recorded and often absent for related species.

Territorial raiding is an alternative route to dulosis that phylogeny alone may not separate.

Collecting pupae as food is a historical function, not a preserved trait.
